back: Thread: one lane running the kernel. Warp: 32 threads in lock-step. Block: threads sharing an SM, shared memory and barriers. Grid: all blocks of one launch.
Single instruction, multiple threads: one instruction is issued for a whole warp and each lane applies it to its own registers.
Lanes of one warp take different branch sides; the warp runs each side in turn with the other lanes masked, so cost is the sum of the paths. Results stay correct.

front: How does an SM hide memory latency?
back: By keeping many warps resident (their registers stay allocated) and issuing from whichever warp is ready, so switching is free.

front: GPU memory levels, near to far
back: Registers (per thread) > shared memory / L1 (per SM) > L2 (whole chip) > HBM global memory (off-chip) > host RAM over PCIe/NVLink. Each step is roughly 10x less bandwidth and more latency.

front: Why is data movement usually the bottleneck?
back: Arithmetic units are far faster than HBM can feed them; kernels with little reuse of each loaded byte are bandwidth-limited.
Consecutive lanes read consecutive addresses, so a warp's 32 loads merge into the fewest memory transactions (1 for 32 aligned float32).

front: Why is walking down a column of a row-major matrix slow?
back: Consecutive lanes are N elements apart, so each lands in a different memory line: up to 32 transactions per warp, most of each line wasted.
32 banks; word w is in bank w mod 32. Different words in the same bank are serialised (m-way conflict = m cycles); the same word is a free broadcast.
Allocate tile[32][33] instead of [32][32]: column accesses then have stride 33 words and spread over all 32 banks.
blocks per SM = min(max blocks, max threads // t, registers // (r*32*warps), shared // s); occupancy = blocks * warps per block / max warps.
